why: Two equal and opposite forces can cancel each other's translational effect only if they act on the SAME body, because only then do they enter the same free-body equation and sum to zero. In (P) the two gravitational attractions form a Newton's third-law pair acting on two DIFFERENT point masses: each mass carries just one unbalanced pull of magnitude \(F = \frac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}\) and accelerates towards the other, so neither force removes the translational effect of the other on any single body. In (Q) both forces of the couple are applied to the same tap along different lines of action; their vector sum is \(\vec{F} + (-\vec{F}) = 0\), so there is no net force and no translation at all — the chapter says a couple is used to realise purely rotational motion. In (R) the weight and the normal reaction act on the same block along the same vertical line, so \(N - mg = 0\) and the block stays at rest; the translational effects cancel completely. Only the gravitational pair between the two separated point masses therefore fails to cancel. The alternative that adds the water-tap couple to it is wrong because a couple has zero resultant force; the alternative naming the block on the table alone, and the one that pairs the tap couple with the block on the table, both pick situations in which the two forces act on one body and cancellation is exactly what happens.

Every one of these is a contact force, and every contact force traces back to the electromagnetic interaction between the atoms and molecules of the bodies in contact. Tension (w) is carried by the inter-molecular bonds of the stretched string. The normal force (x) is the electromagnetic repulsion between the surface atoms of the table and those of the object resting on it. Air resistance (y) is the net result of electromagnetic collisions between the moving body and the air molecules. Buoyancy or upthrust (z) is the resultant of fluid pressure, and pressure is nothing but molecular bombardment, again electromagnetic in origin. Of the four fundamental interactions, gravitation is a separate long-range interaction while the strong and weak nuclear forces act only over nuclear distances of about \(10^{-15}\) m, so none of them is responsible for any of w, x, y or z. Hence all four belong to the electromagnetic family. Each of the three shorter sets leaves out one genuine electromagnetic force — one drops the normal force, one drops the upthrust and one drops the tension — and so is incomplete. The chapter's own classification table makes the same point, listing tension, normal force, friction and the resistive force offered by air or water all under electromagnetic forces.

Equidistant point masses sit at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side \(r\). Each mass is pulled along the two sides meeting at its own vertex, and the angle between two sides of an equilateral triangle is \(60^\circ\), so for every mass the two attractions are inclined at \(60^\circ\) and the resultant follows the parallelogram law, \(F = \sqrt{F_a^2 + F_b^2 + 2F_aF_b\cos 60^\circ}\). Writing every force in units of \(\frac{Gm^2}{r^2}\): the mass \(m\) is pulled by \(2\) and by \(3\), giving \(\sqrt{4 + 9 + 6} = \sqrt{19} = 4.36\). The mass \(2m\) is pulled by \(2\) and by \(6\), giving \(\sqrt{4 + 36 + 12} = \sqrt{52} = 7.21\). The mass \(3m\) is pulled by \(3\) and by \(6\), giving \(\sqrt{9 + 36 + 18} = \sqrt{63} = 7.94\). The largest resultant therefore acts on the heaviest of the three, the mass \(3m\). The claim that the mass \(m\) feels the greatest force confuses force with acceleration — the lightest body does have the largest acceleration, \(4.36\,\frac{Gm}{r^2}\) against \(3.61\) and \(2.65\) for the others, but the question asks for force. The mass \(2m\) is intermediate, not maximum. And the forces are certainly not all equal: although the individual attractions occur in equal and opposite third-law pairs, the two pulls acting on any one vertex have different magnitudes and different directions, so the three resultants differ.

Both forces are inclined at the same angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal, but one pulls the block and the other pushes it, so their vertical components point in opposite senses. For the pulling force the vertical component \(F_1\sin\theta\) is directed upwards and partly lifts the block, so the table need only supply \(N_1 = mg - F_1\sin\theta\). For the pushing force the vertical component \(F_2\sin\theta\) presses downwards and adds to the weight, so \(N_2 = mg + F_2\sin\theta\). The stem states that the maximum opposing force is proportional to the resultant normal force, \(f_{\max} = \mu_s N\), so the block is harder to start moving in the pushing case simply because \(N\) is larger. Setting the horizontal component equal to that maximum opposing force at the point of impending motion, \(F\cos\theta = \mu_s N\), gives \(F_1 = \frac{\mu_s mg}{\cos\theta + \mu_s\sin\theta}\) and \(F_2 = \frac{\mu_s mg}{\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta}\); the second denominator is the smaller one, so \(F_2 > F_1\), which is exactly what the stem reports. The reason is therefore that the vertical component of the pushing force adds to the weight and increases the normal reaction. The statement crediting the pulling force with increasing the normal reaction has the sign reversed, since a pull unloads the surface and reduces \(N\). The two statements that speak of a component adding directly to the opposing force are wrong in mechanism: neither applied force has a component along the friction direction other than the horizontal component that drives the motion, and friction grows only indirectly, through the growth of \(N\).

Take the direction of motion of the heavier body as positive. The mass \(2m\) moves with speed \(u\), and the mass \(m\) is approaching it head-on with double that speed, so its velocity is \(-2u\). The total momentum before impact is \(2m(u) + m(-2u) = 2mu - 2mu = 0\), and since the collision force is internal this stays zero afterwards: \(2mv_1 + mv_2 = 0\), that is \(v_2 = -2v_1\). The coefficient of restitution compares the relative velocity of separation with the relative velocity of approach along the line of impact, \(e = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{u_1 - u_2}\). Here the approach speed is \(u - (-2u) = 3u\), so \(0.5 = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{3u}\) and \(v_2 - v_1 = 1.5u\). Substituting \(v_2 = -2v_1\) gives \(-2v_1 - v_1 = 1.5u\), so \(v_1 = -0.5u\) and \(v_2 = +u\): both bodies rebound, each having reversed its direction. Their speeds after the collision are \(0.5u\) for the mass \(2m\) and \(u\) for the mass \(m\), and a quick check confirms momentum, \(2m(0.5u) = m(u)\), the two final momenta being equal and opposite. Taken in the order in which the stem introduces the bodies, the ratio of their respective speeds is \(\frac{0.5u}{u} = \frac{1}{2}\). The value \(2\) is the same pair of speeds written in the reverse order, with the lighter body first. The value \(3/2\) is the separation speed \(1.5u\) divided by \(u\), and \(2/3\) is its reciprocal; neither is a ratio of the two final speeds.

Let the rod have length \(L\) with a vertical string at each end, and let the boy hang at \(\frac{L}{3}\) from one end, which makes that end the one nearer to him. The rod is uniform, so its weight \(2mg\) acts at the mid-point \(\frac{L}{2}\), while the boy's weight \(3mg\) acts at \(\frac{L}{3}\). Writing \(T_1\) for the tension in the string close to the boy and \(T_2\) for the other, vertical equilibrium gives \(T_1 + T_2 = 2mg + 3mg = 5mg\). Now take moments about the far end, which eliminates \(T_2\) because its line of action passes through that point: \(T_1 L = 2mg\left(\frac{L}{2}\right) + 3mg\left(L - \frac{L}{3}\right) = mgL + 2mgL = 3mgL\), so \(T_1 = 3mg\) and hence \(T_2 = 5mg - 3mg = 2mg\). Checking with moments about the near end confirms it: \(T_2 L = 2mg\left(\frac{L}{2}\right) + 3mg\left(\frac{L}{3}\right) = mgL + mgL = 2mgL\). The required ratio is \(\frac{T_1}{T_2} = \frac{3mg}{2mg} = 1.5\). The value \(2\) is what the boy alone would produce on a massless rod, since his load divides in the inverse ratio \(\frac{2L/3}{L/3} = 2\); including the rod's own weight, which splits equally as \(mg\) and \(mg\), pulls the ratio down from \(2\) to \(1.5\). The remaining two values do not follow from any consistent balance here — whatever the ratio, the tensions must add to \(5mg\), and \(3mg\) together with \(2mg\) is the only such pair that also balances the moments.

Three of the four alternatives are restatements of the chapter's own list of characteristics of the centre of mass, which is what identifies the odd one out.

The claim that a force whose line of action passes through the centre of mass exerts no moment is characteristic 4 of that list: the centre of mass is the point at which, if a force is applied, it causes only linear acceleration and not angular acceleration. Referred to the centre of mass, which is the natural reference point for a free body, the moment is \(\tau = r F \sin\theta\) with \(r = 0\), so it vanishes and the body merely translates. The claim about balancing on a pivot is characteristic 11 almost word for word, that while balancing an object on a pivot the line of action of the weight must pass through the centre of mass and the pivot. The claim that an open arc-shaped uniform rod has its centre of mass off the rod is characteristic 16, that the centre of mass need not lie within the body: for a uniform circular arc of radius \(R\) subtending a half-angle \(\alpha\) at its centre of curvature, the centre of mass lies at a distance \(\dfrac{R\sin\alpha}{\alpha}\), and since \(\dfrac{\sin\alpha}{\alpha} < 1\) for every \(\alpha > 0\) that distance is strictly less than \(R\). It therefore falls short of the arc itself, in the empty concave region.

That leaves the assertion that the Earth's centre of mass is not at its geometrical centre, and this is the statement that does not stand. What moves a centre of mass away from the geometrical centre is an ASYMMETRIC distribution of mass, not merely a density that varies from place to place. The Earth's density does rise steeply towards the core, but it does so in essentially spherically symmetric shells, and every such shell has its own centre of mass at the common centre; the polar flattening is symmetric about that same centre. Summing the shells therefore puts the Earth's centre of mass at its geometrical centre to well within a kilometre out of a mean radius of \(6371\) km. The residual lateral density variations are far too small to make the printed claim true, so denying that coincidence is the wrong statement about the centre of mass.
_adjudication: Blind pass concluded the moment-through-centre-of-mass statement. Overturned by hand against section 4.13.4: characteristics 4, 11 and 16 underwrite three of the four options, leaving the Earth claim as the only one the chapter does not assert.

why: The chapter states the condition sharply: the centre of mass lies at the geometrical centre for a symmetric rigid body OF UNIFORM DENSITY. Both halves of that condition must hold. An egg (I) fails both — it is an ovoid that is broader at one end rather than symmetric about its middle, and shell, albumen and yolk have quite different densities, so its centre of mass is pulled away from the mid-point of its long axis towards the broader, denser end. A cubical box containing assorted sweets (III) has a symmetric container but a deliberately non-uniform filling: sweets of different sizes, shapes and densities heaped in no particular order give a mass distribution with no symmetry at all, so the centre of mass is displaced from the geometrical centre. These two are the unambiguous cases. The cylindrical box full of rice (II) is the marginal one, and it is worth being explicit about why it still belongs: rice is not a continuous medium but a heap of discrete, irregularly shaped grains that settle into a random packing, with the finer broken grains and dust working their way downwards, so the actual mass distribution is not symmetric about the mid-height of the cylinder and the centre of mass does not sit exactly at the geometrical centre. Only an idealised filling of genuinely uniform density would place it there. So all three of the listed objects qualify. Of the shorter alternatives, the one naming only the egg and the one naming only the sweet box each discard an object that visibly fails the uniform-density test, while the pairing of the egg with the rice box omits the assorted sweets, which is the most obviously non-uniform of the three; none of these three can be right.
